utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, everyone. I think that our teams are the same as this morning. I should like to ask the registrar to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The case number, IT-98-29-PT, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Prosecution, the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This afternoon the Office of the Prosecutor is represented by myself, Michael Blaxill; and I am joined by my colleague, Mr. Stefan Waespi; and Ms. Annink-Javier is our case manager, who is also at the table. Your Honours, may I just add one thing, that we were today to be joined by Mr. Mark Ierace, our new senior trial attorney, who will have the overall conduct of this case. He has been in post since Monday of this week, and tragically this afternoon, at lunchtime, he received news of the death of a relative back in Australia through an accident, and with that sudden and tragic news he had to leave the Tribunal immediately to make his way back to Australia for family reasons. So on his behalf and on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, I offer his regrets that, through tragic circumstances, you are still denied meeting the senior trial attorney who will be conducting this case before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. We really regret the circumstances through which we have been denied the presence of your lead counsel. I hope that things will improve shortly. For the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Nikola Kostic, appearing with General Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. In application of a Scheduling Order of the 4th of October, 2000, the Status Conference today will be divided in two parts. There will be a hearing on the motion for the Trial Chamber to travel to Sarajevo, in particular the progress that has been made in the negotiations between the parties as regards a draft protocol of the envisaged visit. That is the reason why I, as a Pre-Trial Judge, am joined by my two colleagues today, Judge Riad and Judge Wald. After that, there will be a Status Conference which is convened in application of Rule 65 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, for the purpose of discussing the progress that has been made in view of the preparations for the trial. We will begin with the discussion on the motion for the Trial Chamber to travel to Sarajevo so that my colleagues can be excused after that. Thereafter, I will indicate the agenda for the Status Conference, and perhaps between two parts of the hearing today we can have a short break. As you know, the motion was submitted by the Prosecution and bears the date of the 14th of July, 2000. According to the motion, it is suggested that the Trial Chamber travels to Sarajevo and to its immediate surroundings. The envisaged date for the visit would be sometime between the filing of the Pre-Trial briefs and the opening of the trial itself. Considering the fact that the Trial Chamber was inclined to carry out such a visit, and in view of the fact that, according to the Prosecution, the Defence has not expressed any opposition to the idea, the Scheduling Order of the 4th of the October, 2000 suggested that the parties submit a draft protocol for the Trial Chamber site visit to Sarajevo. The set protocol should include certain details, such as the exact locations of the visit, the guarantees regarding the rights of the Defence, and also a suggestion as regards the modes of communication between the parties and the Judges. The protocol should be completed as soon as possible so that necessary arrangements can be made, unless otherwise decided by the Chamber. So I should like to hear the parties about the progress that has been made in that respect and I should like to begin with the Prosecution. Mr. Blaxill, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm obliged to you, Mr. President. We have, in fact, prepared an initial outline draft of a form of protocol, a copy of that was dispatched by post on the 6th of October of this year to my learned friend, Mr. Kostic, but I understand from him today he says he hasn't received it. It is, however, a short document and contains nine very short paragraphs. So I think he's probably had time for a quick and probably a fairly thorough perusal at this point. Your Honours, I would like to submit a copy of that for your own perusal just to help follow any discussion, but I have to say at this immediate point in time, as we had perhaps hoped maybe to have heard Mr. Kostic in-between times, we have not taken the step of having this translated into French. Had it been something we'd formally wished to submit to you, of course, we would have tried to comply with that as I know it is something that the Chamber rightly desires. But in essence, I think, Your Honours, our view is that certainly the Prosecution feel an on-site inspection of the environs of Sarajevo would assist the Tribunal greatly. It would help Your Honours to understand particularly the unique topography, as we see it, of Sarajevo and its surrounding country. It's our submission, Your Honours, which may be I'm, to use an English expression, teaching granny to suck eggs, and I don't mean to, but of course, we believe you can exercise such a function under Rule 4 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence with the blessing of the President of the Tribunal. Since the exercise is viewed by the Prosecution and no doubt by Your Honours as a judicial function and I think has to be exercised as a judicial function, it is appropriate, we feel, that the -- there should be some set guidelines and/or indeed rules for particularly communications between the parties, or more particularly, the parties and yourselves. Indeed, the fourth paragraph of our draft protocol does suggest that, prior to any visit to the site, there should be a written itinerary suggested, and I think that's something where, in my anticipation, we would have various places that the Prosecution would wish you to see and various places that the Defence would wish you to see. I know your fellow judges in the Kupreskic trial had anticipated such a visit in their case and I know, for security reasons, that didn't occur. But indeed I think, quite effectively, they invited all parties to submit the particular areas of interest and then they were able to work out an itinerary for that. I think that also assists very much in that if one has to use any form of local guide in the situation, it can avoid any influence being brought to bear through a third party because Your Honours would have a firm and clear view of where you wish to go and what you propose to see. I think with those written requests being put in, it should be feasible, perhaps by negotiation between Prosecution and Defence, to even suggest some of the logistics for an itinerary. In this case, you do have a city that is within a defined valley and there are basically a couple of east-west roads and one north-south road which form the kind of skeleton of the place. It is not difficult to get around, and I think an itinerary can easily be achieved for you. With regard to communications, again the suggestions which we have put together essentially are that, obviously, the parties may have a need to draw something to Your Honours' attention but, of course, it has to be essentially to do with the location and the topography of the place not, of course, to try and indulge in arguments on merits of the case before you in such a circumstance. And also that possibly one way to ensure that the propriety of communications with Your Honours is observed is that through a court deputy who is with you, or an appointed officer, we would first, as it were, filter the communication through them and they could then see to it that the appropriate communications reached Your Honours. The other factor would be the presence of the parties during any communication. We feel it is an appropriate safeguard that clearly, if one party wishes to make a representation to Your Honours, then the other party should be present. Now, on that basis, I think probably within a few days we could put together and we've had -- I have personally had some thoughts on the idea, to put together some practical suggestions for an itinerary, and with the presence of Mr. Kostic here now, I'm sure we could hammer out something quite quickly that would help all parties make some logistics decisions and be able to go forward with preparations certainly sufficient for Your Honours to consider an order and for the President to consider his authority. There may be other -- obviously, other logistical considerations, namely the cooperation of the entities of the area and any concerns by SFOR as to how these things should proceed. But on that basis, we certainly, from the Prosecution point of view, are very much minded to ask you to consider favourably so doing, and I think it is a feasible undertaking in this particular case. The final thing, Your Honours, is that really the manner of recording. Two options have been considered in the past. Whether you have periods of audio-visual recording with a video camera on site so that when you are looking at specific locations, it is actually viewed, the parties are present, and it is recorded both audio and visual or, and in conjunction with, written minutes with the locations visited and any communications with Your Honours. Maybe the video thing is more comprehensive and a better option for recording the visit than simply written minutes. But those are the suggestions we've committed to paper so far, so -- unless there is a question you have for me at this stage, Mr. President, or Your Honours, perhaps you might care to hear the views of Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Blaxill. Thank you very much for your suggestions. We will perhaps, my colleagues and I, have questions later on but I should like to hear, first of all, the reaction of the other party. We know already that Mr. Kostic did not perhaps have enough time to think about this proposal but, however, we would like to hear your initial response, albeit a temporary one. You don't have to tell us anything as a definitive answer, but let us hear your answer on the proposal. Mr. Kostic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: When I initially received the motion and it was filed at the time when Mr. Terrier was the senior counsel, we actually had a conversation about the motion before it was actually filed. I told him at that time, and I'm repeating that statement to the Trial Chamber now, that anything that would assist the Trial Chamber in understanding various aspects of the litigation that's in front of you, the case that you're going to be dealing with, I think is something we ought to try. I told Mr. Terrier that this idea of a Court or a Tribunal or a Chamber visiting a certain scene is not necessarily unusual where I practice. We call this a jury view if it's a jury case, and I think Mr. Blaxill has done that in the past. Obviously, some of the cases in the national jurisdiction are a bit more narrow and not as complicated as what is involved here, but that is perhaps why I feel that the motion is appropriate and I think that, if the Trial Chamber is to visit the area, that it would help the Trial Chamber to follow the evidence in this case. When I talk about evidence, I'm thinking not only in terms of the fact that you may be receiving into evidence maps, photographs, videotapes, perhaps, as is mentioned in the motion, some kind of a relief map and so on, but I still think when you are able to visit a location, it is very, very helpful. So in principle, I felt that it was appropriate and that I could support that particular notion. I will get back to the fact that I do have some other reservations and matters that I want to deal with in regard to what I think the Trial Chamber ought to see. But before we go into that, I think one thing that I agree with Mr. Blaxill is the fact that this is a very obviously serious and somber procedure, this litigation, and I would hope, and I know -- I certainly know the Chamber will work very hard not to have that visit be anything but a judicial function. To be honest with you, my concern would be that it would turn into some kind of a media situation and so on, and I would hope that we could avoid -- I'm sure we can avoid that. But I just wanted to voice that at this time. I also agree with Mr. Blaxill that since we're going to be visiting the territory of two entities, Republika Srpska and the Federation, that at some point fairly soon there ought to be some coordination with the appropriate authorities in those two entities to assist us. When I'm saying "assist us," I'm speaking now as an officer of the Court here; in other words, assist the Trial Chamber in making sure that everything is done as well as it can, that security is guaranteed, and again -- and some of the other reservations I had. So I think that Mr. Blaxill is correct that we do need to consult with those two entities. I'm not about to suggest to Your Honours or to the President of the Tribunal how to do that. I think you've done that for a number of years and I'm sure that that can be accomplished. So that, I think, is something that I think you need to know. I have looked -- and I have to be very honest with you, I've only taken a very quick skim of the draft protocol which is in your possession now, and I think that we can discuss that also perhaps, and I may have some comments. One matter which I do want to share with you initially which I'm concerned about, and this sort of ties into Rule 4, of course, but it also ties into Article 21 of the Statute of the Tribunal. That's Article 21(4)(d), which talks about the rights of the accused. And as you know, that particular paragraph deals with the fact that the accused has the right to be tried in his presence, as I'm quoting from that particular Statute, which raises the issue, and that is: How do we characterise the Trial Chamber's visit? Is it a part of the litigation, a part of the judicial process? Is it a part of the trial of General Galic? Because if that is how we characterise it, then I think, under Article 21(4)(d), he would need to be present, and I think that is an issue which has to be dealt with by the Chamber. I know that, of course, it raises maybe additional security issues and other aspects, but I think you should be mindful of that and we can, I'm sure, discuss that. And then finally, as I have looked at this protocol, draft protocol, Mr. Blaxill has worked out what seems like an outline where essentially the parties would provide written suggestions of an itinerary, the places they want to visit, what they want the Chamber to see. I think what's going to happen, practically speaking, is this: I think that Mr. Blaxill and I and the rest of the Prosecution team will probably agree on a number of sites that you ought to see. And I think we can agree on that and I think that will not cause us to have to contest issues. There may, though -- there may be locations and the width of your visit in terms of geographic areas and specific sites where we may -- the Defence may say we absolutely need to see these, we would urge the Chamber to do so, whereas Mr. Blaxill may feel that it isn't necessary to see them, for whatever reason he might have, of course. And of course, on the other hand, we may have some feelings about a list that he would provide. So I think we're going to be dealing with three categories of locations, some we can agree on and then the other two areas that we can't. Mr. Blaxill and I spoke just before we went into this session, and I know that probably as early as tomorrow we'll be able to sit down and at least find an area that we can agree on, and of course work on the other areas. But that, Your Honours, is sort of generally something that I would like you to consider, and obviously if there's a need to submit any kind of writing, even a memorandum in regard to the issue that I presented to you, I would be happy to do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kostic. I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Blaxill for his response, but anyway, I should also like to inject these views. The Chamber would be inclined to agree with this visit if this visit will indeed save us time, witnesses, the duration of the testimony of witnesses, and so on. You must understand that the Chamber is not interested in a tourist visit. It is indeed a working visit. But we have to see what will be the consequences in terms of the expediency of the trial, bearing always in mind the question of fairness. This is, I would say, in my personal opinion -- of course, my colleagues will have an opportunity to express their views -- I think that we truly need to view this visit in the context of shortening trial time. If we come to that conclusion, then we probably will be inclined; if not, we will not be inclined. Because, as you know, the key issue at the Tribunal now is the question of Judges' time, so we have to use that time as effectively and efficiently as possible. Having made that remark, I give the floor to Mr. Blaxill to respond to the observations made by Mr. Kostic. You have the floor, Mr. Blaxill, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think in one area I would agree with my learned friend when he says there's probably going to be three sorts of categories of things. One is where the Prosecution suggest you should see points A, B, and C, and he would agree; we might say D, E, and F, and he will not agree; and others will be the other way around. However, I think that in essence, if we are setting this up in the sense that this is a geographic exercise for orientation, which I think would save Your Honours' time -- I think it saves time when locations will be described to you -- it can just, even if it foreshortens a number of witnesses by a few minutes, over a long trial that can end up with hours and even days of saved time. I think, therefore, again, if we do submit this kind of prior itinerary that can be scrutinised by Your Honours first, I think you will be able to identify instances where if you feel we are going into an effort to influence a view of evidence, then I think it would become apparent. And I think if we simply are stating locations within the town and that nobody is trying to influence you as to what we say about those locations, then I think we serve the purpose, and I think that is a very feasible and, in fact, an easy task. The other issue that my learned friend has raised, and this is the question of the Article 21 rights of the accused, well, to that extent, as to the existence and propriety of these rights, clearly I would not argue for one split second. It is probably one of the most ancient rights in most places of the world that a person accused may face his accuser. What I'm saying is that the city and the hills around it are not the accuser; they are simply the locus in quo. We have a location. It is geography. And no one seeks to try and convict General Galic on the strength of geography. So I think that, again, with the appropriate safeguards we may have suggested, if they appeal to Your Honours, I think we have a situation where the Article 21 rights of the accused are well protected and well served by the presence of his counsel and by, let us say, if nothing else, the restriction upon the Prosecution even to make any kind of representation to you in the absence of legal representation on the part of Mr. Kostic. So on that basis, I do not feel that, in my personal view, that we risk jeopardising or compromising the letter or the spirit of Article 21 and the -- indeed, the enshrined right of an accused to be tried with all elements in his presence. It is a restricted visit for geographical awareness and I know we would consider it no more than that. So those would be my representations on those two issues, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, I have just a small question. You really raised two important points: saving time and acquiring geographical awareness. Now, these two cannot be compensated by videotapes showing us the area, that we save more time and give us the geographical awareness? I mean, suppose I want to have geographical awareness of Australia. Do I need to go there or can I have it on the maps and in videos or films?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I don't attempt in any way any sort of flippant humour in what I'm saying, Your Honours, but I've seen films of Australia and I have been there, and there is no substitute for the experience. I think when it comes to perceptions of distance, of light, of height, and of your perception of surroundings, I do not believe that the camera cannot lie, and I do not believe that the camera is a substitute for the human experience. I say I have no legal precedent to offer you to support that remark, but I honestly believe, and it is my personal experience of Sarajevo -- it is probably the personal experience of Mr. Kostic -- that when you go to a place, you can experience far more than any amount of videotape or -- because you have 360-degree vision, just like this, which you still can't do with a camera, not fully. So I would suggest, for the sensory perceptions, there is still a distinct advantage in being on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I was going to ask Mr. Kostic, who referred to his experience in his own jurisdiction with site visits, and I've had a little bit of that. In my experience, the accused didn't go on them. Is your experience different?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in -- I can honestly tell you that I think on every jury view that I've gone on, the accused or the defendant was there. I know that, on occasion, the judge in question was a little concerned, especially if you're dealing with a very serious charge and so on. For me, though, even though I would have gone to this site previously by myself, as Mr. Blaxill and I have gone to Sarajevo more or less by ourselves or in -- so on, sometimes it is helpful to have your client with you in those circumstances which I'm sort of indicating. The other is I am concerned when I read the statute and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's why I asked you. As you are well aware, in the United States, we have a similar guarantee of the public trial and the right of an accused to appear before. We can certainly research the jurisprudence to find out if there's been any, but I know I've been in at least one where the defendant was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of the things that does concern me is that I don't think it's been done before, to my knowledge, within this particular jurisdiction. So we are sort of embarking on something new and if you or the rest of the Chamber would like me to look into that and you think you might be helped by providing you some -- obviously, it's going to come from other jurisdictions -- I would do that, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have already heard the views of the parties. For the moment, I think that we have said that we must continue between -- with the conversations between counsel so as to perhaps reach a memorandum or maybe these three categories of sites to be visited; a category on which the parties will agree, another category that the Prosecution would like to visit but not the Defence, and vice versa. That is to say that we need to have a document, signed by both parties, specifying the points on which they agree, the points that one side would support and is opposed by the other. I think that is what we need to do. With respect to this question of jurisprudence, I think that the Tribunal is going to adopt its own jurisprudence. That is to say, I think it will be the first time for a Chamber to travel to make an on-site visit to the sites mentioned in the indictment. It is true what Mr. Blaxill said that there was another attempt which, unfortunately, did not take place for reasons of security. I think that we need to consult the security service to see whether we can travel and under what conditions. In any event, I would like to express my personal opinion. I think that it should be done on condition that we are saving time. Otherwise, we will be spending a lot of hearing time showing maps, photographs, videos of the area and the geography. If that would save time, then we should do it. As I have said, everything that we can do outside the courtroom, outside the hearings in the courtroom should be done in order to achieve the balance which has to be always maintained, and that is to have a speedy but also a fair trial. So we have to keep a balance between the two. Therefore, bearing this in mind, the Chamber will make a decision in due time. Perhaps we should now give practical form to this suggestion. I don't know whether for the parties 7 days would be sufficient or whether you need more time to draw up such a memo. I don't know whether that has anything to do with the availability of Mr. Kostic for discussions on this matter. When I said 7 days, I can also say 15 days, but the idea is to go forward as quickly as possible. Mr. Blaxill, what is your opinion regarding the setting in motion of this suggestion of this procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Quite simply, yes, Your Honour. We can, I think, put together what we would propose within a seven-day period and it's -- we're at Mr. Kostic's disposal because we were anticipating, in respect of what has been happening around us, we were anticipating probably that from now until the 26th would be precisely the time to do all this various preparation, subject to what Mr. Kostic says. Your Honour, if I could digress from your question for a moment, I do have in my possession a copy of, and I will pass it to Mr. Kostic, of the order that was in fact made on the 13th of October, 1998, signed by His Honour Judge Cassese which, in fact, sets out a blueprint for the proposed visit that they were going to make in the Kupreskic case and I will happily share that with my learned friend. It might assist us. Clearly, it does seem there is already a precedent set, there is a precedent set in this Tribunal for non-attendance of the accused. And as Your Honour quite rightly pointed out, it was for security reasons that that did not go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Mr. Blaxill spoke about the position of the Prosecution, but we should hear the position of the Defence as well. What is the position of the Defence, Mr. Kostic, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I've said initially, I think, is the statement that I will generally adopt again. I do want to bring up a couple of matters. I've had another look at the draft protocol. I was sort of looking with one eye in and one eye at the draft protocol. I do like the idea that Mr. Blaxill is very sensitive about the fact as to how the communications are dealt with between the Prosecution, the Defence, and the Chamber. I think that's very, very appropriate, and I think that's something that we can easily adopt. Of course, I would be concerned, and I'm sure that the Trial Chamber would be very much not only careful, but would certainly resist any communication from any other sources while there. I don't even have that problem. But I think that's something that we should be aware of because of the nature of the case. I do think that we can continue meeting and, as I said, I will be here and I will continue meeting with Mr. Blaxill. I would like to take a look at Judge Cassese's memorandum or order, whatever it is. The only Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. thing that I'm concerned about is that I would like some guidance from the Chamber in this sense: If we are to prepare lists, you can imagine that they can become somewhat lengthy, and also there is some difficulty in making sure that we are clear on what we would like you to see. And that may not be quite as easy to do as quickly because I think there's quite a number of locations that, between Mr. Blaxill and us, we would like you to see. And for that reason, that may be somewhat troublesome in a sense to do it very quickly. My suggestion would be, of course, to move ahead and to do as much as we can, but to still allow us some additional time to make sure we haven't missed anything in terms of what we would like you to see, or if we are not satisfied with the description of what we would like you to see, that we do that. As you know, places have changed names. Some places are not the same today as they were four or five, six, seven years ago. So there are those situations that I would hope the Trial Chamber can have some -- how should I say -- should give us a little leeway so we can deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that what we can conclude in the sense of guidelines for the parties, that we will have a Status Conference on the 26th of October. The parties may engage in exchanges between themselves to try and produce some sort of a document, and even to have doubts, if one can put it that way, so that we can discuss these matters at the Status Conference, that is, what is the common ground and what are the doubts that you have and perhaps we too will have doubts because, after all, we too would like to participate of the definition of the itinerary and the whole project. So I think that is the best way to proceed on the 26th of October. We'll have, as an agenda item, this to see which of the points the parties agree, which they disagree on, and which doubts that they may have. So now we can go on to the Status Conference proper, but before that, I should like to confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I interrupt you for just one moment? Some other practical point has just crossed my mind and that is that we are in mid-October, and it has been, I think, the experience of anyone with regular visits to Sarajevo and the like that the weather will very much dictate sometimes what one can do, even with getting in and getting out. So, of course, if you are thinking globally of timing and the start of the trial and various other things, I think it is a legitimate consideration as to what season you feel that you would best be able to travel to get the best benefit from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Blaxill. It is always true that we prefer the spring, after all, but it is an aspect of organisation that we need to take into account because that depends on the nature of the questions that we need to observe. As you know, the majority of actions were conducted in the summer because it was not possible to engage in them during the winter. So you see, this is a point that certainly needs to be taken into consideration. We shall now have a very short break of six or seven minutes, and we'll be resuming after that for our Status Conference. --- Break taken at 4.37 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now move to our Status Conference. As far as the Status Conference is concerned, we have at least 11 points to consider. I'm going to inform you of the agenda so that we can bear in mind all of them. First of all, we will consider the disclosure of evidence by the Defence and the Prosecution; second, we will see what the situation is as regards the application of Rule 65 ter, that is, the Pre-Trial brief of the Prosecutor; number 3, judicial notice; number 4, reciprocal disclosure. We will elaborate on that later on. Special defence, any special defence offered by the Defence; preliminary statements; Rule 84. We will also have to discuss whether the accused intends to testify or offer a statement pursuant to Rule 84 bis; the issue of expert witnesses; and also the participation of the Defence in the Status Conference; Article 73; timetable; and any other issues that the parties wish to consider and which have not been indicated as part of the agenda. As it is usual, we will begin with number 1, with the first item of the agenda, that is, the disclosure of evidence by the Prosecution to the Defence. There are actually two issues involved here, and I'm going to mention the first one. As regards evidence which is contained in Rule 66(A)(ii) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, has a solution been found to expedite the proceedings, which was discussed during our last conference? And the second issue is the following: During the last Status Conference, the Prosecution recognised that Rule 68 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence imposes a permanent obligation to disclose on them. I should like to know whether there has been a disclosure of evidence which is covered by this particular Rule so far. So that would be the first item on our agenda, and I should like to hear the Prosecution, Mr. Blaxill, on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regard to firstly Rule 66(A)(ii), I'm going to say that I just have a minor misunderstanding, I think, as to quite what you refer to when you say about "expediting." I'm wondering whether you mean whether we have yet agreed anything, whereby we would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke about the packages that got lost in the process of communication or disclosure of evidence. We discussed it last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. We were duly supplied, I believe, safely received by my learned friend. So that is no longer a problem, as I understand, Your Honour. Yes, that's taken care of. With regard to Rule 66(A)(ii), we have only, in fact, a modest amount, and I would say a modest amount, of evidence currently being dealt with vis-à-vis the lifting of a Rule 70 restriction. Once that is dealt with, and I believe it can be dealt with certainly well before the November conference date, of course it will be served promptly upon its release. As regards any other additional evidence that may be coming in, or perhaps evidence that may substitute for other evidence, there is about to be a -- I was going to say substantial disclosure, but in cases of this size it is not that substantial. The fact is that, over the last four weeks, our investigative team has been recontacting the civilian witnesses in Sarajevo, and basically a number of these people were interviewed back in 1995. So, clearly, it was appropriate to go back to them. Now, as a result of that, we have found perhaps one or two witnesses who are now not so well, not so able to travel. We have had reported now two incidents of deceased witnesses. My learned friend will be informed, when we meet, about those situations. And we have also undertaken the task of taking statements prepared in the language of the witnesses which reflect the statements they previously gave to the Tribunal. The purpose of that has been to get them to adopt their evidence, make any corrections, and perhaps overcome a problem that has been encountered in other trials, where a witness in court has heard what is stated in a statement taken in English and then later disagrees. It's caused some frictions and problems, so we're endeavouring to overcome them. Now, as a result, my learned friend will be getting further disclosure in the next couple of weeks. They are being entered into evidence now. They will then be drawn and served on him, in compliance with Rule 66(A)(ii). All of this stuff will essentially be a repeat of what he has had, but it is now brought up to date and we know which witnesses are still ready, willing, and able to come and testify. There may be some instances where we will, in due course, as a practical matter, Your Honours, be asking you to consider possibly the question of deposition or affidavit evidence for specific people, for specific reasons, but in that respect we are, therefore, I trust, up to date on our obligations under 66(A)(ii). With regard to Rule 68, at this time we are undertaking searches with that very specifically in mind. I understand, if my understanding of the Rules is correct, that our duty is to disclose, not necessarily to sort of put up a flag that it's Rule 68 that we're doing, but where this is sufficiently clear, I think it is perhaps appropriate, to assist my friend, that we would do so, and I think we will do so. In appropriate cases, we will try and batch this together and let him have it under that guise. But we are conscious that this is an obligation that runs, and it will simply, if we come across such evidence, it will be served as it is found. Now, in that regard, and taking account of it as a disclosure issue, on the last occasion I informed Your Honour that a large search was being undertaken. The last count, I'm told, was something like 2.5 million pages of material being scanned by a large team, and elements of that get referred to the relevant trial teams. The amounts received thus far are not that daunting, I'm pleased to say, but nevertheless we do have this ongoing project; and in fact, due to a number of quite considerable computer and logistic problems, the flow of information only really started in earnest last week. On that basis, we will have an ongoing disclosure of relevant material and Rule 68 material, which I think will go until this task is completed. It's beyond our control, in that sense, but obviously we're mindful of our duty and we will stand by it, and we will consistently serve particularly Rule 68 material as soon as it's in our hands. So the process, I would like to say in encapsulation, is ongoing. There is a new batch of Rule 66 material to go into my learned friend's hands in the very near future. And in essence, as regards evidential disclosure, that's the case. And yes, the missing boxes were delivered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Blaxill. Mr. Kostic, do you wish to respond in respect to these two items? Have you indeed received the last boxes and have you received all of the documents, or are you still waiting for some documents to be disclosed, in particular, those covered by Rule 68?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive the items that were missing, and I think that's not an issue any longer. I have received some other documents which are documents that are of subsequent interviews. I should tell you also that Mr. Blaxill and I have met in September on a number of occasions while I was here, and pretty much what he has reported to you just now he and I discussed at that time, so I am appreciative of the fact that he is making the effort to supply the Defence with the Rule 66 material, as well as the 68. But the only thing that I understand, and of course I accept his representations, and that has to do with this rather large -- what would you call them? -- 2.5 million pieces of paper, for lack of a better term, that they're working on that and that I'm sure that that is going to be done at some point. In fact, I think I've met some of the people working on that. So I think that there's an effort being made, and I'm sure that he will be supplying me with the materials as they come. And then, finally, the Rule 70 materials he told me about. I have a general idea what is being done with that. I'm satisfied that that's being done according to the procedures, and I'm expecting to receive that. So I guess on that issue, Mr. Blaxill and I do not have any issues at this time to report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we have covered these two items. However, before we finish this discussion, I have to tell you that the Chamber is trying to stabilise, so to speak, the case before it actually opens. We understand and we know that the Prosecutor is still continuing with her investigations and that new disclosure is always possible. However, in terms of organisation and the functioning of the Tribunal, including the fairness and the expedience of the trial, one has to note that if the Prosecutor has issued an indictment, it means that she's ready for a trial. Having said that, the Chamber will be strict in application of its authority. I don't wish to have any surprises later on, because in some other cases we have had the situation where the Prosecutor changed his list of witnesses at the very end of his case, which caused us a significant amount of problems. What we are trying to do during this Pre-Trial stage is to stabilise the case as much as it is possible. So once the trial opens, it opens for a case that has already been prepared. I have to therefore remind you, and I think that this is very important in terms of objectives that are enshrined in the statute, in terms of the accused, the accused has the right to a speedy and fair trial. So if we keep changing witnesses' statements, the Defence is not in a situation to prepare themselves and cannot properly fulfil and discharge its obligations because we have to review the position and start from the beginning once again. So what we need to do during this pre-trial stage is to have a certain commitment by the parties because it is not fair for the accused to have a number of changes occurring all the time during the trial stage. But we will have another Status Conference. We will have another chance to get prepared. There are always exceptional circumstances, I grant you that, but the Prosecutor has to get organised before the beginning of the trial. So we will be discussing everything. We will prepare the case during this pre-trial stage, and then the case will really open. The trial will really begin. I don't know if there is anything you wish to say or comment in respect of this strategy that I have exposed to you, both in terms of theoretical and practical aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think with the cases that come before the Chambers of this Tribunal, Your Honour, quite frankly, stability and a sound, prepared case is something which is desperately desired by all. I speak as now an advocate in now two prior cases that such is a situation that nobody likes any kind of disorder to set in one, it's a tough enough task to work on something from start to finish that is well prepared. I think one of the problems that has arisen probably over the last 12 months is not exclusive to the position of this particular case is that we have seen, and to an extent, some of that is public news, that the regimes have changed, the climate has changed, and in that respect also, that means that the results of investigations that are ongoing, not necessarily we're trying to investigate this case, but the reality is that we are coming into possession of document collections and other things which raise two very specific points. On the basis of a fair trial, I would commend to Your Honour that clearly one has to be fair to two things. I always assume the Prosecution tries to represent the truth. So if we find something that adds to the truth, we have a duty to try and put it before you. Secondly, of course, there's Rule 68, and if somebody in the course of investigations shall access an archive of, say, some military force or some governmental part of an entity that's now opened up to us for some reason, then, of course, we would have that ongoing duty as well. So I think I heard a colleague once say that trials in this institution have a certain sort of dynamic life to them just by the nature of the background to the whole thing and where the cases come from. But I think within the parameters of those problems, some of those things can actually help the Tribunal greatly, and the Chambers can learn a fundamental truth that may not otherwise be so explicit to them. So, obviously, we are mindful that we want to be straight, we want to have everything in order, and get on with our job. And I think, speaking as an advocate, I would rather be in court than in an office so I would rather the trial obviously to start and we can get on with our business. But I do caution, if I may be allowed to caution you, Your Honour, that these are the other dynamics in the world, and we would be fooled in our duty if we said, "Well, we have got this package, we will proceed and ignore these other things." But naturally, we will try to keep any inconvenience to the system and to the Chamber to a minimum, but I think that is a fair position, from our point of view, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Blaxill, we will accept your caution, but you also have to accept ours. The Chamber will try and do its best in terms of discussing the issues and preparing the issues that will come up during the trial phase, and once the trial begins, the most important role will be, of course, the role of the witnesses. But we both take note of these reciprocal cautions that have just been expressed. Let us move to the second item of the agenda, that is the provisions of Rule 65 ter. In terms of order of the 4th of October, the Prosecution has until the 7th of December to fulfil its obligations stipulated in the said Rule and the Defence has to meet its obligations pursuant to Rule 65 ter (F) by the 14th of December, 2000 at the latest. That is the pre-trial brief. I should like to know if there has been any progress made regarding the adjudicated facts in application of paragraph (ii) and (iii) of Rule 65 ter (E). During the last Status Conference, the parties informed us that very little progress had been made in that respect, and I do hope that such a situation has improved in the meantime, despite certain problems that we had with the timetable. The Chamber should therefore like to hear the parties on this particular issue, and I'm going to give the floor first to the Prosecution and then to the Defence. Mr. Blaxill, has any progress been made regarding stipulations and agreements between the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I would like to think that we are on the eve of, Your Honour, because I have already agreed that I shall be meeting my learned friend tomorrow 0930 and I have been keeping basically all days between now and the 26th of October clear for whatever demands this case places for such purposes. With regard to judicial notice, we had, in fact, set forth a schedule which was dispatched to my learned friend but I know he didn't receive it in the post. We found out there was a technical reason for that and that will be remedied. In that particular document, there is 237, I think, but please don't hold me to the figure, something in that region, of adjudicated facts that we have drawn from the decisions in the Tadic and Celebici cases, in particular, and which we are putting forward as particularly factual proposals as which we invite my learned friend to comment on and we would then propose to incorporate in a motion for judicial notice. So basically, as soon as my learned friend Mr. Kostic and I have had a conversation about this, we will be in a position to motion the Chamber on the issue of the judicial facts. So taking account certainly of the fact of the 7th of December deadline, I am confident we shall be more than ahead of that deadline. Regarding other matters of stipulation of fact by agreement between the parties, I have also prepared a list and I think, yes, my colleague kindly indicates it's something like 96 factual propositions in there. It's thus not a long document, and I am submitting the same also to Mr. Kostic so that we can consider between us what facts he may agree with for stipulation to the Court. So to that extent, again, I think it will be a very short time now before we have our areas of agreement and disagreement pretty much mapped out. Subsequent to that, we have to weave that into the pre-trial brief. Already, the legal structure is completed. Much of the factual structure is in place in terms of our approach, of course, and it really next will need anything to be woven in, in terms of what will be agreed or disagreed as between ourselves. Now, again, we are, thus far, I hope I'm not hanging myself here, but we are confident that we are heading comfortably to the date that has already been set to the 7th of December for compliance of 65 ter in all those respects. So unless you have a specific question, I think that's all I have to say on that point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much, Mr. Blaxill. I think you have moved to our next item on the agenda, the judicial notice, but before we broach that particular subject, I should like to give the floor to Mr. Kostic to respond to what Mr. Blaxill has just said. I know that tomorrow you will have a meeting, but could you tell us now if there is any agreement as regards factual and legal issues, and since the judicial notice has been mentioned by Mr. Blaxill, if there is anything that you wish to state in that respect as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm awaiting to receive the documents that Mr. Blaxill referred to, so there's very little I can add. I do envision one issue when dealing with the issues on stipulations and judicial notice which will be the facts that will be drafted, and that is that, with the other documentation that's coming in that we have to do, my concern is in having the client review those facts. Because, after all, any stipulations, any agreements, any judicial notice agreements would have to have the consent of the client. The issue there, of course, is being able to have the client read that in his language. So that, I'm going to say, is something that I'm going to have to -- we're going to have to deal with, and I'm hoping that my friend from the Prosecution will help me with that issue. But other than that, I have nothing else to add other than you know we have already told you that maybe about five times already that we are going to get together tomorrow morning, so I won't repeat that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So at least we know that tomorrow you are going to meet and I should now -- the volume of the microphones is very strong today -- I should like to go back for a moment to the provisions of Rule 65 ter in order to mention that the pre-trial brief pursuant to 65 ter (E)(i) we have always said that it should be the result of conversations, communications and exchanges between the parties. Therefore, the working instrument that the Prosecution spoke about last time, we can conclude that it is in that stage and the parties need to meet to see where we stand in relation to that instrument. So I can go on to the next agenda item, the list of witnesses that the Prosecution intends to call in accordance with 65 ter (E)(iv). You have told us that you intend to call 180 witnesses. In the scheduling order of the 4th of July, we ordered the Prosecution to try and limit the number of witnesses to two per fact. The Trial Chamber may envisage a schedule within which each party will be accorded a limited amount of time for the presentation of witnesses, regardless of the number of witnesses it intends to call. So I think, Mr. Blaxill, we have reached a stage when, as I have already said, we have to be expeditious and fair, and as I have also already said, the problem at the Tribunal here today is the problem of Judges' time, judicial time, so I repeat we should do as much as we can outside the courtroom. That means that we should bring to the courtroom the witnesses who are essential for defining the responsibility of the accused. The majority of other things can be brought to the trial through affidavits, through deposition testimony, through transcripts from other trials, testimony given in another case can be brought here. But here, of course, we have to discuss matters because what may occur is that Defence counsel may have questions for that witness but the Chamber is going to keep that under control. We will see which other new questions being put to the witnesses because, unless there are no new questions, then that transcript of testimony can simply be entered into the record. Then there's also the question of expert witnesses, and if we keep to this idea that we bring into the courtroom witnesses who have to do with the heart of the matter, the responsibility of the accused, then perhaps we would be able to reduce the number of witnesses on one hand and, on the other, to reduce the time for the presentation of evidence here in the courtroom. Something else that perhaps we should take into consideration right now, we are talking a lot about reducing the number of witnesses but perhaps we could look at another possibility and that is how we can reduce the time of each testimony here in court. I have some suggestions to make to the parties for their consideration but, for the moment, are you going to stick to this number of 180 witnesses, Mr. Blaxill? I can see already that your answer is no. So what is the number going to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, I'd hoped you might have accepted the no without another number, Your Honour, because the reality is that we are going through that witness list with essentially two things in mind. Firstly, where we can do without the witness because we simply have more than we need, and, in that respect, we are being mindful of Your Honour's comment at the last Status Conference when you said that the Chamber would take what is becoming, I think, a fairly normal practice that two witnesses per fact is enough. Now, we have a fairly substantial number -- let's say one of our areas of witnesses at the moment contains probably 30 names, people who would give a large picture of events in the cities in view of this nature. And it is something that I will discuss as soon as I'm -- my trial leader returns, because at the end of the day I would like him, I think, in fairness, to have a considerable say in that kind of strategy as to which of the witnesses he feels are significant for the case he's leading. But we would be looking at maybe a half a dozen out of 30 to be of assistance to the court and we would not necessarily need to trouble any more. We have other areas the same, where perhaps you have witnesses at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. different levels of authority who may have had contact with several persons that prove a point. Now, we can choose: Do we have to call one, two, or three of them? No, we would probably find one of them and say, "Well, that is sufficient." So I think there will be a considerable -- I'm confident there will be a considerable paring of the list. I'm confident also that we will be submitting and suggesting to Your Honour, and with my friend's leave, the use of affidavits for a number of witnesses, where I think their evidence is perhaps less contentious or where perhaps there is maybe only one question that would be asked, and that question would hold good for all those people and maybe there would be some way around that. So the answer is no, we do not anticipate the number that was previously expressed. And really and truly, again we are setting our sights that probably we will be in a position to elucidate more accurately as to numbers by the time of the November conference, where you scheduled I think the 27th, and that would be, on the basis of our final list, ready for filing on the 7th of December. So I think -- sorry, I believe it's the 17th of November. My mistake. I'm obliged. So perhaps I could leave it at that. It may not be an entirely satisfactory response today, except I know we will dramatically reduce the list, and we take on board everything Your Honours have had to say about it today and before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Blaxill. We are cautioning today, and of course forecasting things, speaking in advance, so it's normal that we should be cautious. It is true that the Chamber has given this guidance of two witnesses per fact, but you should have a list of reserve witnesses, should you need them. So that is the other side of the coin. I think that is the reasonable thing to do. We're saying two witnesses for each fact, yes, but we're also saying you can tell us that you have a reserve list of witnesses and, if necessary, you will call them. So I'm giving you this indication for the moment. I suppose that the Defence has nothing to say at this point. Am I interpreting correctly your position, Mr. Kostic? In that case, we can go on to the exhibits. And I think that there is a problem there. The Prosecution has said that it needs to discuss with the Defence the authenticity of documents in order to determine in which cases those documents are contested, or rather their authenticity is contested. I would like to add that I was about to put this possibility before the parties. You know there is a practice of bringing a document by a witness and then the witness will say this and that about it. I think that it is not necessary to bring witnesses to say that the document says such-and-such. We can read the documents. But what may happen is that there is an important question that is raised by the document, in which case one needs to have a witness. So I think perhaps you could consider the possibility of documents speaking for themselves, and witnesses will come related to those documents if that is really necessary. In that way, we could overcome the question of authenticity, so that we can organise all the documents in cooperation with the registrar, so as not to waste time here in the courtroom. If things are well prepared in advance, one can save a great deal of time, courtroom time. So authenticity and this question of allowing documents to speak for themselves. Mr. Blaxill, your comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: To that extent, I'm wholly in accord with what Your Honour is saying. In the preparation of our exhibit lists and in dealing with documentary evidence, we are endeavouring to ensure that, to the best level that it can be established, the authentication of the document has been done. Now, on that basis, it is a possibility, I would hope, that if we say we want to use a specific document, then it quite -- is conceivable that there would be perhaps no objection by the Defence if we have shown that, in the background, we do have the authentication evidence. It is an issue I will discuss with Mr. Kostic. And that means, at least, that if we have the evidence, we'd only call it if we had to, but otherwise, we could just simply seek admission of the documents. The Rule, I think, confused me very slightly in that the obligation under 65 ter appears, Your Honour, to be that we should file our list of exhibits by the due date, say the 7th of December. But of course, I anticipate -- and in fact, I've not imagined it, because I think my learned friend mentioned it in one connection in the last Status Conference -- that of course it's very difficult to ask for comment on authentication on the basis of a list. I imagine Mr. Kostic would be in his rights to say, "I want to see the document before I say whether I agree on its authentication or not." But having said that, even if the Rule itself does not, we have discussed this and we will do our best to disclose those documents in advance of time insofar as we can so that he can consider the authenticity issue. We are in preparation of that. Again, we have the same target date, and again I propose talking to Mr. Kostic on that specific issue whilst he is here between the two Status Conferences. Hopefully, we can get a workable result that will have things in good order by the 7th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kostic, have you any comments to make on this matter? Because we really need to speed things up to finish by 6.00 at the latest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a very short comment. I just want you to understand that Mr. Blaxill and I have talked about this. We understand the issue. And he is right that I would like to see the document in question before -- not only myself, but of course with the client's assistance, to make sure that we make a decision on whether we can stipulate to the authenticity or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On my agenda which I read to you, I have the issue of judicial notice. Mr. Blaxill mentioned the possibility of judicial notice, using evidence from Celebici and the Tadic case. I should like you also to consider the hearing 61 regarding Karadzic. Have you considered that possibility, taking those materials as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I've thought about it, Your Honour. Certainly they are materials that have come before this Tribunal and they are materials that have come before us on solemn declaration in an open hearing. The difference between the Rule 61 hearing and a trial is, of course, that that is not evidence that is tested by a Defence, it is not evidence adduced for the purpose of detention or acquittal of an accused, and it is connection with the issue, essentially, of international arrest warrants. So I have not at this stage resorted to that particular judgement as being one for the judicial notice prospect. Perhaps it's something, I must say, I would sort of look to Your Honour's guidance as to whether the Chamber would be happy with that particular scenario and give my learned friend the opportunity to comment, because there is that subtle difference-- well, quite considerable difference between a Rule 61 hearing and, of course, a formal trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We are in agreement, Mr. Blaxill. But in the area of contested issues between parties, we could always consider all available material. I should like to hear Mr. Kostic on this point, though, whether there is any point in considering this possibility as an issue of discussion, whether we can gain anything from it, and if so, how.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree with Mr. Blaxill's interpretation in regard to the different types of hearings in question, but I'm also concerned with the issue of the confrontation of witnesses, of course. So, obviously, I think I would not be happy to have that type of evidence come in, generally speaking. But you do have to realise that I'm not sure if I know all of the evidence that had come in during the Rule 61 hearing, which occurred, I think, maybe some four years ago. Obviously, if Mr. Blaxill feels that he wants to take advantage of that, we will treat it as we have with the other matters, and I will have a chance to object and you'll hear that objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should nevertheless like the parties to bear in mind, yes, there is a difference. The evidence under Rule 61 hearing were not tested, to use that expression, by Defence counsel. Other transcripts and testimonies were put to the test. But there is at least something that one can discuss between the parties: Is there something that I can accept? And another part that I do not accept I will put to the test. We have said regarding the transcript testimony from other cases given under oath, we have said that they were put to the test by the Defence counsel, and only then can we accept new questions, so as to avoid any repetition, to make the best of what we have, without repeating things. So all these persons could come not to repeat what they have already said but to respond to questions that may be put to them regarding new matters and new questions. That is an idea that I would like to put to you for you to consider. Perhaps I should speed things up a little, because we have only reached the third item of the agenda among the 11. Maybe I could list the matters and you can prepare a response. The next point is item 4, reciprocal disclosure in accordance with Rule 66(B) and 67 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I think it can be noted that the parties have still not discussed this, but they will do so. At the last Status Conference, we thought we understood that the Defence requested the disclosure of evidence in the possession of the Prosecutor, pursuant to Rule -- of the accused to Rule 66, and the question raised was whether reciprocal disclosure will be resorted to pursuant to 66(C). I know your reply will be that we still haven't discussed this. So we come to special defences in 67(A)(ii). The Defence told us last time that the Defence will reserve the right to invoke the defence of alibi. I should like to remind you that 67(A)(ii) refers to certain obligations of the Defence, and these obligations have to be carried out as soon as possible and, in any event, prior to the beginning of trial. We're inclined to apply this Rule in a rather strict manner in order to avoid the useless presentation of evidence and repeating an experience that we had in another case. So we have to bear in mind that if there is a defence of alibi, that it already exists in the case. So it is at this point, that is, before the trial, that it should be invoked or not. That means that after the beginning of trial, I am telling you, I am warning you, that it would be very difficult for the Chamber to accept. I'm saying this so that things should be quite clear for the transcript. Therefore, Mr. Kostic, do you still have this idea of invoking the defence of alibi or do you wish to think about it until the beginning of trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it all depends if there's any additional information that I receive from the Prosecution. The reason I think I reserved it the last time is that we still haven't got all the information. I can tell you that -- boy, I don't want to -- I don't want to be like a weatherman and give you a prognosis. It's more likely that we will not use that, but I want to reserve it at this point, just to make sure, until all of the discovery materials come in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The useful conclusion would be that, Mr. Kostic, you must bear in mind that Rule 67 is quite clear in saying that notification of this defence must be made prior to the beginning of trial. So we come to opening statement. Perhaps it is still very early, but in any event, it is another matter that the parties must think about. For the Prosecutor, it has been customary for him to make an opening statement at the opening of trial. As you know, regarding the Defence, you have the possibility of choice: Either you make an opening statement at the beginning, or not. If you do make an opening statement, again you have a choice: either to do it immediately after the opening statement of the Prosecutor or after the completion of the Prosecution case and before the beginning of the Defence case. And to speed things up, the answer of the Prosecutor regarding whether he will have an opening statement is yes. Can he confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's yes. The microphone wasn't on, but I saw him nod. And Mr. Kostic, what about you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will make an opening statement. I do -- I have to make some calculations that have to do with length of the trial and other matters, whether we will make it in the beginning, right after the Prosecutor's, or we will reserve it until the beginning of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received an interpretation saying the Defence -- let me look. Yes, fine. The next question, perhaps it is too early to raise it, but we are trying to plan all these things and, in order to plan, we have to take into consideration all possible elements. Perhaps it is too early for the Defence to answer this question, but is the accused going to testify? That is our first question. Is he going to make a statement pursuant to the provisions of Rule 84 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence or will he not be doing either?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Galic does intend to testify, and I'm quite certain it will be done during the Defence case in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that he intends to testify, only to testify? As you know, there are two possibilities. To testify is one, and to make a statement pursuant to Rule 84 bis is another. When you say that he is going to testify, does that mean he's not going to make the statement provided for by Rule 84 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I think you are correct. I think it's going to be a straight testimony during the Defence case, a question and answer testimony during the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in any event, perhaps we should leave this matter open and you can talk to General Galic about it and see what his opinion is. In any event, that question will remain outstanding until the next time we meet, Mr. Kostic. The next point that we need to address is the question of expert witnesses. The Prosecution has notified its intention to call six expert witnesses and it has already communicated some of their reports to the Defence. This is what the Prosecutor told us at the last Status Conference. I should like to recall that Article 94 bis of the rules stipulates that the findings of expert witnesses should be communicated as such to the opposing party as soon as possible and shall be filed with the Trial Chamber not less than 21 days prior to the date on which the expert is expected to testify. This rule also requires that the opposing party, within 14 days after receiving the report of the expert witness, should file notice whether it intends to cross-examine the expert witness or not. My question is: Is there any news regarding this point, Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Not really, Your Honour. As regards a couple of the potential experts, we are trying to identify still a couple of disciplines where we want to get the most appropriate for the case as such and, in any event, obviously, we are fully mindful of the rules and they will be served appropriately and likewise filed with the Chamber appropriately. Having said that, the other initial experts that we had have, in fact, been served but we have not resorted to that rule at this stage but we have included that but identified within the 66(A)(ii) material. So at least my learned friend has had them. He has had them for some considerable time. However, because we have not highlighted these statements as and, in fact, I don't think at this stage they are somewhat preliminary, I don't think they are in a form I would wish to see as being filed as the report, so on that basis, clearly I would not wish to in any way try and hold my learned friend to any specific response in respect to those statements. They are essentially to alert him to the content of the evidence and a little later, when all else is done as regards witnesses, we will then obviously propose to serve the fully prepared reports as such and then we can go through the necessary responses and filing that is appropriate under the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I don't know whether Mr. Kostic has anything to add on this item.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you haven't. Thank you very much. So we go on now to item 9 of the agenda and that is the participation of the Defence as provided for by Rule 65 ter (F). I'm not going to repeat what I have already said at the last Status Conference. In any event, there are here at least three points through which the Defence should contribute to this pre-trial conference because, afterwards, we will have a pre-trial Defence conference at the end of the Prosecution case in chief. Those points are the kind of Defence of the accused, the matters which the accused intends to contest. I am not going to ask you, Mr. Kostic, whether you already have a response for these three points, but I wish to convey to you some wishes of the Chamber. As you know, the work of the Defence is done by the Defence, but the key issue is the responsibility of the accused in relation to the indictment. As you know, there are a whole number of facts and background information in the indictment which does not directly concern the accused. So there may be a certain area of agreement, judicial notice or acceptance of certain facts in part, at least. Otherwise, if you do not agree, you should tell us which are the reasons for you taking issue with these things. I am joking a little, but I am quite serious too. The more agreement there is, the less reasons you have to provide. Of course, that affects the Defence of the accused and his right to defend himself but, after all, the crux of the matter is his responsibility. Do you have any comments or reactions at this stage, Mr. Kostic, or would you like to reserve your comments for later, after giving the matter greater thought?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have thought about just the question that you've asked. Obviously, much of our thoughts on it are based on the information we have received, the research we have done, and the discovery materials. I think we will, and I'm cognisant of the procedure that we're going through, in other words, the attempts to reach some perhaps agreements on some issues. We will be able to tell you whether we agree or we do not agree on some of those facts, and I think that will, in some way, build a skeleton of the Defence. So I think you will have some idea as to that. So I am mindful of that obligation. We will do that. My only concern is that your order gives us seven days between one and the other and I would think, unless Mr. Blaxill and the Prosecution has an objection, I would appreciate obtaining more time in that regard, mainly because we do have a little bit of a break right after that which you are not -- well, at least I'm told that the Tribunal is on vacation. I would like to take advantage of that time to get a little more time to do that. Because parallel with doing that particular task, dealing with the obligations here, as you know, we'll be dealing with all of the other obligations in terms of judicial notice in terms of stipulated facts, reviewing the witness statements and so on, and that would be helpful to the Defence. I would sort of orally move the Court to give us some additional time. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kostic. I thought I heard that Mr. Blaxill would facilitate your task because he indicated that he would not only meet the deadline but submit it in advance. We will see what will happen at the next Status Conference. For the time being, we will stick to the timetable that is already suggested. As I have already indicated, the plan is as follows: We impose time limits and deadlines. We will have deadlines and time limits for the whole trial. We will say we will finish on such and such date. We, of course, have to do our best in order to respect those deadlines and time limits. However, if there are exceptional circumstances, if something unexpected happens, we are always available to discuss matters. But we have to proceed with deadlines and time limits in advance. The parties have to know the opening and the closing date of the trial, and we also have to know how much time is necessary for each particular stage of the trial so that everybody who is working on the trial can plan both their private and professional agendas. We will see if Mr. Blaxill is able to submit the necessary filings prior to the set deadline. We will see. If he is able to do that, so much the better. But for the time being, we will stick with the timetable that has been suggested. The timetable is something that is useful for us to proceed with our work but we need not be slaves of that timetable. The next item on our agenda is actually the timetable, the calendar. There will be a Status Conference on the 26th of October, as it has already been agreed. You have enough time to work. The idea was to give you as much time as possible for you to meet together and to discuss the matters. So this time is for you to meet and on the 26th of October, you will tell us the results of your meetings. And if necessary, will you inform us on your future meetings and there will be another Status Conference on the 27th of November, 2000. At this stage of the proceedings, I should like to tell you that the pre-trial conference which is covered by Article 73 bis is scheduled for the 23rd of January, 2001, Tuesday. We have to have everything ready before that and the pre-trial conference, as far as things stand now, is scheduled for the 23rd of January. As I have already indicated, the Chamber intends to be as strict as possible during this preparatory stage of the proceedings and provide you with necessary guidelines during the trial itself. Maybe we will need one additional date to continue the pre-trial conference because I'm sure that a lot of issues will have to be discussed. So for the time being, we have the date of the 23rd of January for our pre-trial conference. If it is necessary, there will be a continuation of the pre-trial conference afterwards, if necessary, of course. And this brings me to item 11 of our agenda, namely to see whether there are any additional matters which the parties wishes to raise. Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Just one I would like to raise with Your Honour at this time. And that is this: It is in respect of the filing of any particular pleadings, notices, or the like in the course of proceedings. I am conscious of the wholly appropriate fact that Your Honour wishes to have documents prepared, legal pleadings and the like, to be filed in both the English and the French language or the French and the English languages.
